title: Ukraine Strikes Deep Into Russia, Pakistan Swat Bombing Kills 14, Ceuta Death Toll Rises to 72
subhead: Ukrainian drones hit targets 1,300km inside Russia as both sides escalate long-range attacks; a suicide bomber kills 14 at a Pakistan anti-violence rally; and the Ceuta migrant crisis leaves 72 dead as EU scrambles for a coordinated response.

sections.heading: Ukraine Strikes Deep Into Russia as War Escalates on Both Sides
sections.body:
Ukrainian drone swarms struck targets across Russia overnight, killing at least nine people according to regional governors, with hits reaching as far as Udmurtia — over 1,300km from the front line. Ukraine's military said it attacked the Saratov oil refinery and the Engels strategic bomber airbase, sparking fires at both facilities, as well as an oil depot in the Kaluga region. The Engels airbase, home to Russia's strategic bomber fleet, has been repeatedly targeted by Kyiv. A residential building in Engels was struck, killing two people, according to regional governor Roman Busargin. Three people were killed by a drone strike on a car in Udmurtia, whose acting governor called the act 'monstrous in its senselessness.' In the Belgorod border region, four people were killed, including a 13-year-old girl near a playground. Ukraine also struck its 12th Wildberries logistics warehouse since July 18, targeting the company it describes as a linchpin of Russia's consumer economy that supplies drone components to the military.

On the Ukrainian side, at least five people were killed by Russian attacks on Sunday. A guided bomb struck a residential building in Zaporizhzhia, killing one person. Another attack killed one person and set fire to a postal terminal outside Kharkiv. Two died in Dnipropetrovsk and one in Kherson. Russian forces also struck Ukraine's largest online retailer Rozetka's warehouse overnight. According to AFP data compiled from Ukrainian Air Force reports, Russia fired a record 376 missiles at Ukraine in July — more than double June's total — with most aimed at Kyiv. President Zelenskyy warned of a critical shortage of US-supplied Patriot interceptor missiles, saying air defences intercepted 154 drones but only one ballistic missile in the latest barrage. US Patriot interceptor stockpiles have fallen from about 2,300 before the Iran war to fewer than 827, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies, raising concern about coverage gaps on multiple fronts. (Sources: Al Jazeera, BBC, AFP)
sections.whyItMatters: Both sides are investing heavily in long-range strikes far beyond the front lines, but Ukraine's ability to sustain air defence is eroding as interceptor supplies shrink — a problem compounded by US munitions being diverted to the Iran conflict.

sections.heading: Trump Claims Deal 'Perimeters' Agreed, Halts New Iran Strikes
sections.body:
President Donald Trump announced early Sunday that he would hold off on ordering new strikes against Iran, claiming that Middle Eastern allies had reached the 'perimeters of a deal' to end the five-month-old war. 'Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL,' Trump wrote on Truth Social. He said the deal would include 'the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran's nuclear threat,' adding that Israel had joined the commitment.

The announcement came hours after Trump had declared the US 'locked and loaded' and ready to strike at levels 'not seen since World War II.' The reversal followed a phone call from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman urging Trump to 'prioritise dialogue' and de-escalate, according to the Saudi Press Agency and Axios. Iran denied requesting any pause. Iranian state media, citing military officials, called Trump's claim 'nothing but a new lie,' insisting armed forces remained on high alert. Iran's acting defence minister said Tehran treats every threat as 'real and credible' and will 'neither be caught off-guard nor remain passive.' (Sources: AP, Al Jazeera, BBC)
sections.whyItMatters: Trump's pattern of dramatic escalation followed by sudden de-escalation has repeated multiple times in this conflict. The gap between his claims and Tehran's statements leaves enormous uncertainty about whether diplomacy or another round of strikes comes next.

sections.heading: Hormuz Negotiations Enter 'Final Stages' as Iran Pushes New Maritime Route
sections.body:
Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said negotiations with Oman on the Strait of Hormuz are entering their 'final stages,' describing them as 'on the way to being finalised' in a report to Iran's cabinet. Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said Tehran and Muscat were close to reaching a deal on a new maritime route through Hormuz — separate from existing corridors — that would 'respect the sovereign rights of both sides and safeguard our national interests and security.' The details of the proposed route remain unclear.

Crucially, Baghaei said the new route 'has nothing to do with whether the Strait of Hormuz is reopened or remains closed,' blaming the US for the waterway's closure. Iran's position remains that Hormuz will never return to its pre-war status. Ships remain stuck in the northern corridor in Iranian waters, with the IRGC-affiliated Fars outlet reporting they can only pass if Iran's armed forces permit. Meanwhile, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Fox News the US was pursuing a permanent geopolitical shift away from reliance on Hormuz, arguing regional states now see Iran as an active threat. But analysts note that existing bypass pipelines can handle only about 9 million barrels per day of the 20 million that normally transit the strait, and shifting routes to the Red Sea simply moves the vulnerability to Bab al-Mandab, where Houthi forces threaten shipping. (Sources: Al Jazeera, AP, EIA)
sections.whyItMatters: Even if a new route agreement is reached, it would give Iran continued leverage over transit — and any alternative corridor still faces the Houthi threat in the Red Sea, meaning the global energy disruption has no quick fix.

sections.heading: Ceuta Death Toll Rises to 72 as EU Calls Emergency Meeting
sections.body:
The death toll from the Ceuta border surge has climbed to 72, with five more bodies found along the enclave's coastline on Sunday. More than 1,000 people have been treated by health services since the influx began on Thursday, when approximately 60,000 people — mostly Moroccan nationals — crossed from Fnideq and Belyounech into the Spanish territory. While over 48,000 have since returned to Morocco, the crisis has triggered a political chain reaction across Europe. Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni suspended Schengen open-border travel with Spain, and France has tightened its border with Spain. Twenty-two EU member states have called for coordinated border action, and the European Commission has convened an emergency meeting.

Spain has installed a 500-metre floating barrier off Ceuta's coast and rejected claims that its migrant regularisation programme encouraged the crossings, insisting those who entered irregularly cannot travel to mainland Spain or elsewhere in the Schengen zone. Morocco's Interior Ministry attributed the surge to misinformation on social media, human trafficking networks, and misinterpretation of a Spanish Supreme Court ruling banning immediate returns of migrants intercepted at sea. Far-right politicians and activists have descended on Ceuta, but local residents pushed back, shutting down an anti-migrant rally on Saturday. (Sources: Al Jazeera, BBC, NYT, AP)
sections.whyItMatters: The Ceuta crisis has exposed the fragility of Europe's border architecture and Schengen system, with Italy and France already taking unilateral measures. The political fallout — including the rise of far-right mobilisation — could reshape EU migration policy for years.

sections.heading: Suicide Bombing Kills 14 at Anti-Violence Rally in Pakistan's Swat Valley
sections.body:
A suicide bomber killed at least 14 people and wounded 22 outside a police station in Kabal, in Pakistan's Swat Valley, striking near a crowd that had gathered to protest the region's escalating violence. According to Swat District Police Officer Umar Khan, the bomber detonated explosives after police attempted to stop and search him at the entrance of the police station. The blast tore through the crowd as a speaker addressed the gathering, sending panicked residents fleeing.

The attack comes amid a sharp escalation in violence across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. Just three days earlier, an ambush using explosive-laden drones killed 11 police officers at a checkpoint in Hangu. A car bombing in nearby Tank killed 27 soldiers in late July, an attack claimed by the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan. Researchers at the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies recorded 154 terrorism-related deaths across the province in July — more than double June's toll. Pakistan has repeatedly accused Afghanistan's Taliban government of sheltering armed groups that plan cross-border attacks, a charge Kabul denies, and the dispute has fuelled Pakistani air strikes on Afghan territory earlier this year. No group has claimed responsibility for the Swat bombing. (Sources: Al Jazeera, Dawn)
sections.whyItMatters: A bombing at an anti-violence rally underscores the accelerating TTP insurgency in northwestern Pakistan. With 154 deaths in July alone and attacks employing drones and vehicle bombs, the security situation is deteriorating rapidly — and the cross-border dimension with Afghanistan raises the risk of wider conflict.

sections.heading: Gaza Strikes Kill 13 Despite Hamas Disarmament Agreement
sections.body:
Israeli strikes on Gaza killed at least 13 people, including several children, Palestinian officials reported, in the second consecutive night of bombardment. Gaza's Civil Defence Authority said attacks hit Gaza City, Khan Younis, and Deir el-Balah. The IDF said it was targeting military operatives, claiming it killed two Hamas commanders — one from the elite Nukbha force and one from the Maghazi Battalion. A father, mother, and their nine-year-old son were killed in a strike on a house in Khan Younis, and a man and woman died in a strike on an apartment building in Deir el-Balah.

The strikes come days after Hamas accepted a disarmament plan that would see the group hand over its weapons to Trump's Board of Peace, as part of the second phase of the US-brokered Gaza ceasefire. A 15-point roadmap published on Friday sets out steps for implementing the agreement, including inventorying and storing heavy weapons and military infrastructure. But Israel remains deeply sceptical of Hamas' willingness to disarm. Israeli Energy Minister Eli Cohen said Sunday that no deal had been reached to stop attacks on Gaza, and far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir dismissed the draft as 'not acceptable.' According to UN estimates, more than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed since the supposed ceasefire took effect last October, and Gaza is now roughly 70 percent under Israeli control. (Sources: BBC, Reuters, Al Jazeera)
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between the disarmament framework on paper and the reality on the ground in Gaza continues to widen. Israeli officials are publicly dismissing a deal they have not formally rejected, while strikes continue — making implementation of any disarmament process increasingly unlikely.

bottomLine: A day of sharp contrasts: Trump abruptly halted threatened strikes on Iran, claiming deal 'perimeters' with no visible agreement on the core issue of Hormuz — where Iran is pushing a new controlled route rather than reopening the waterway. Ukraine hit targets deep inside Russia, even as its air defences are stretched thin by depleting Patriot stocks. In Pakistan's Swat Valley, a suicide bomber attacked an anti-violence rally, killing 14, as the TTP insurgency accelerates. The Ceuta migrant crisis has claimed 72 lives and fractured Europe's border consensus. And in Gaza, Israeli strikes killed 13 despite a nascent disarmament deal that Israel's own ministers are dismissing. The common thread: on every front, the distance between diplomatic frameworks and ground reality keeps widening.
